capabilities: Encrypt notes and attachments into .sealed files that never exist as plaintext on disk
Edit encrypted Markdown and text in place and render decrypted images and PDFs
Store logins in a built-in secrets manager with groups, tags, custom fields and templates
Issue recovery keys and change the master password without re-encrypting files
Decrypt containers with a standalone Node script, independent of the plugin
extras: Early release, not independently audited and not yet in the community catalogue; the author advises starting with data you can afford to lose, creating a recovery key first, and running the built-in self-tests. Requires Obsidian 1.8.7 or newer; keyring.json must be synced between devices; documented threat model explicitly excludes malware on the machine and other Obsidian plugins.
problem: Vault files sit on disk as plaintext, so a stolen device, a leaked git repository, or a synced or backed-up folder exposes every note and stored login.

relations.evidence: Without -merge, git will attempt a three-way merge on ciphertext and destroy the file.
Syncthing cannot merge an encrypted file either, so it leaves a second copy named …sync-conflict-….sealed.

summary: File-level encryption for notes and attachments behind one password, with a built-in secrets manager, on desktop and Android.
